_meta.scope: open-source doctor · COSMO intent-coverage ontology (public, built on the COSMO paper spirit)
_meta.note: COSMO (Amazon's commonsense knowledge graph, WWW 2024) has no official audit weights. This is a community concept-coverage check, NOT an official COSMO score. It measures whether a listing speaks to user intent across 4 commonsense dimensions, so sellers can spot listings that only stack product-attribute words and ignore why/for-whom/how users actually buy.

dimensions.use_case: where / what the product is used for (scenario + utility)
dimensions.goal: why the user buys it / what outcome they want (COSMO's signature dimension — often missing from attribute-stuffed listings)
dimensions.constraint: limits / qualifiers (when/where it does NOT apply)

_meta.scoring: score = target-line weighted (like alexa); coverage_ratio = matched/total (honest precision). goal is intentionally hard — low goal coverage flags attribute-stuffed listings.
_meta.matching: dual-mode: agent_semantic (preferred, reading extraction_guidance) or substring (fallback, reading _common word lists)

extraction_guidance._instruction: You are analyzing an Amazon product listing to identify COSMO intent concepts. For each of the 4 dimensions below, read the listing text and identify: (1) which concepts are COVERED by the listing (the listing expresses this concept, through any wording), (2) which concepts from this dimension are MISSING (important user-intent concepts that the listing does not address). Do NOT just match keywords — understand what the listing is expressing semantically. A listing that says 'keeps your cat fed while you're at work' covers the work scenario even if the word 'work' doesn't appear. A listing that says 'perfect for your morning jog' covers the running scenario. Do NOT fabricate concepts that are not genuinely relevant to this product's category. Return your analysis as a JSON object with covered_concepts and missing_concepts per dimension.

use_case.definition: Where / what the product is used for — specific scenarios, environments, activities, and contexts of use. Look for: location nouns (office, gym, kitchen, home), activity descriptions (commuting, hiking, cooking, studying), and time-of-use or occasion signals (night, weekend, summer, party).

audience.definition: Who the product is for — target user groups, demographics, skill levels, and roles. Look for: demographic nouns (men, women, kids, children, seniors, baby), role/identity nouns (professional, student, athlete, beginner, expert), and implicit audiences revealed through wording ('fits small hands' → kids, 'boardroom-ready' → professionals, 'busy multi pet owners' → pet owners).

goal.definition: Why the user buys it / what outcome or benefit they want — user goals, desired feelings, results, and pain-point resolutions. This is COSMO's signature dimension: most listings only describe product attributes, not user goals. Look for: benefit verbs (protect, organize, relax, focus, relieve), result adjectives (comfortable, clean, bright, safe, warm, cool), and outcomes described through phrases ('no more tangled cords' → convenience, 'wake up refreshed' → restfulness, 'never miss a meal' → reliability). A single listing passage can express multiple goals — extract them all.

constraint.definition: Limits, qualifiers, conditions, and requirements — what the product can/cannot do, where/how it applies, and trust/durability signals. Look for: capability qualifiers (waterproof, cordless, rechargeable, portable), use boundaries (indoor-only, up to 200 lbs, for dry hair only), material/design constraints (BPA-free, machine-washable, heavy-duty), and usage requirements (needs WiFi, requires batteries). Also capture trust signals that affect purchase decisions (non-toxic, eco-friendly, easy to install).
